00 — Context

What ACKO Drive
Service Centre actually does

ACKO Drive Service Centre (ADSC) is Acko's own network of multi-brand car workshops — offering periodic servicing, accident repairs, denting, painting, and detailing, with transparent pricing, trained technicians, and genuine parts.

Every part of the experience is designed to run without a phone call: digital job cards replace paper estimates, a customer can approve every step from their phone, and the two things people worry about most with any garage — cost and honesty — are handled in the open, on-screen.

01

Free pick-up and drop — a rep collects the car and returns it once work is done

02

Real-time repair tracking and estimate approval, built into the Acko app

03

Online booking with transparent pricing, from around ₹3,999 for a general service

01 — Validate

Proving the need,
before building anything

ACKO Drive Service Centre began as a Labs-style bet inside Acko — a new experiment, not a guaranteed roadmap item. Before any real product effort went in, I helped prove that customers actually wanted this.

FAKE-DOOR TEST

Designing a dummy entry point before designing the real one

Rather than build and launch on faith, I helped design a fake-door test: a dummy booking entry point that looked and felt like a real product, put in front of Acko's own existing users through a targeted coupon — leveraging trust and reach the brand already had, instead of paying to find users cold.

The only goal was to see if real people would take a real step toward booking a car service from Acko, before a single production screen existed.

Existing Acko users
→
Coupon-driven entry
→
Dummy booking page
→
Real intent measured
→
Demand validated
17%CLICK-THROUGH RATE ON THE FAKE-DOOR ENTRY POINT
The actual fake-door screens — a "coming soon" page and a discount voucher, used to measure real intent before the product existed
GROUNDING THE VALIDATION IN THE REAL BUSINESS

Understanding the garage before designing for it

Alongside the fake-door test, I spent time understanding the actual service business: visiting the Acko garage in person, interviewing the operations lead, booking a real service with a competitor to feel their flow first-hand, and running a teardown of how other car-service brands structure their booking journeys.

01

Visited the Acko garage with visual and content design, and interviewed the person running day-to-day operations on infrastructure and process.

02

Returned a month after launch for a second round, this time pulling real operating signals: service mix, turnaround time, and where customers hesitated.

03

Booked and sat through an actual GoMechanic service myself, to feel a competitor's flow first-hand instead of judging it from screenshots.

04

Ran a structured teardown of how the booking journey is built across Indian and international car-service brands.

INSIGHT 01

Customers didn't need price certainty up front — they needed logistics certainty. What stopped them wasn't "how much," it was "what happens to my car next."

INSIGHT 02

Trust in a multi-brand garage is local, not brand-wide. A review count from a city the customer doesn't live in convinces no one.

Demand was real before a single screen was built. That gave us the confidence to launch in one city first — and design the rest as we learned.— from my project notes
02 — Define

Designing a promise
that gets earned in person

With demand validated, the challenge became designing an experience that builds trust without ever showing a fixed price upfront.

PROBLEM 01

Can't quote it blind

Beyond a basic periodic service, no repair can be priced without a physical inspection. A conventional "pick a package → see price → checkout" flow was off the table — it would promise something the product couldn't deliver yet.

PROBLEM 02

Trust has to be self-serve

The flow had to work with no salesperson on a call to reassure a hesitant customer. Every ounce of trust-building had to be designed into the screen itself.

THE MODEL I DESIGNED FOR

One clear path from booking to service

The end-to-end experience I was designing had to hold together as one honest sequence: the customer books first, the car reaches the garage, an advisor inspects it and shares a clear quote, and only once the customer approves does the work begin.

Book service
→
Car reaches garage
→
Advisor inspects
→
Shares quote
→
Customer approves
→
Service begins
GOAL 01

Make the ask feel logistical, not transactional

GOAL 02

Build credibility locally — garage by garage, not brand-wide

GOAL 03

Design a system that scales visually without breaking consistency

03 — Design

Three doors in,
one honest way through

This is the core of what I designed: an information architecture, a booking flow, and a communication layer that never asks the user for a decision the product can't yet support.

IA — ENTRY POINTS

Splitting the funnel by certainty, not by service

Instead of "which service do you want" — which assumes a diagnosis the customer may not have — I designed three parallel entry points based on how much the customer actually knows about their problem, and launched all three together in the first version of the product.

Garage landing page
→
Periodic Services
(routine care)
Specific Repairs
(known issue)
Not Sure
(needs triage)
→
Booking flow
The three entry points, as shipped — landing page through vehicle detection
FLOW DECISION — LOGISTICS BEFORE PRICING

Selling the trip to the garage, not the repair

Since no price could be shown before inspection, I designed the booking step to sell the logistics of reaching Acko, not the repair itself: Pick & Drop, where Acko collects the car, or Reserve Slot & Self-Drop, where the customer drives in. Both are effectively free to book — a refundable ₹400 hold, credited straight back into the final bill once the service is done, rather than an added cost.

That framing mattered: it turns the ask from "pay us" into "hold your spot," which is a much easier first step for someone who hasn't decided to trust you yet. The same screen sets expectations upfront — a dedicated service advisor, and free rescheduling or cancellation up to 12 hours before the slot.

The actual screen — "Effectively FREE for you," ₹400 held and adjusted into the final bill
Vehicle confirmation and the package pricing comparison, as shipped
A FIRST FOR ACKO

Designing the first full video-led hero section at Acko

To build credibility before asking for anything, I designed each garage's landing page around a video of that specific location's infrastructure, in place of static photography — the first time a full-bleed video hero had been used as the primary visual anchor anywhere at Acko. It became the seriousness cue the rest of the page built on, and the pattern was later picked up by other teams across the company.

HERO — VIDEO
▶
Garage-specific video hero — replacing static photography as the landing page's trust anchor
DESIGNING THE LAYER AROUND THE BOOKING

Communication, tracking and support as part of the journey

The booking itself was never the whole design problem. I designed the confirmation screen to surface the assigned garage and advisor with a direct line to talk to them, alongside a tracking view so the customer always knows what stage their car is at, and a support path for when something needs a human. All three were designed together, not bolted on after the flow shipped.

"Why are we asking users to make a payment before seeing the slots and allocated garage?" — a real question I had to answer with the screen's own copy, not a meeting: confirming slots were open that day and through the week, and that the preferred slot comes right after.
LAUNCHING THE MVP

Shipping to one city, and reading the numbers

The first version of this flow launched in a single pilot city — deliberately small, so I could treat it as a live test rather than a finished answer. It worked: visit-to-lead conversion moved from 33% to 55% almost immediately after launch, which is what justified investing further in the full V1 build.

33% → 55%VISIT-TO-LEAD CONVERSION LIFT AFTER THE MVP LAUNCH

HOW EACH VERSION WAS SHAPED

Designing on a continuous feedback loop, not a single research phase

Rather than treat research as a one-time step before design, I kept it running through the whole build: talking to customers directly, watching session recordings of real bookings, and reading heatmaps of where people hesitated or dropped off. Each version of the journey responded to something specific one of those methods surfaced.

User interviews
Session recordings
Heatmaps
Direct customer feedback
WHERE IT LANDED — V1

What 16 iterations added up to

By the time the journey reached V1, the numbers had moved well past the MVP's early signal: a 212% uplift in serviceable-user conversion over the pre-redesign baseline, and an 82% booking success rate — most people who started a booking were completing it.

212%UPLIFT IN SERVICEABLE-USER CONVERSION
82%BOOKING SUCCESS RATE AT V1
05 — Scale

From one city
to a design system

Once the journey held up in its first city, the design problem changed: could the same experience — and the same visual quality — hold up nationwide, without a bigger design team? As sole design owner of this phase, I rebuilt for scale.

  • Revamped the end-to-end mobile and desktop IA and UI, closing the usability and content-visibility gaps I'd identified from the first city's launch.
  • Built a modular, templatized component system specifically for city and locality pages, so new markets could be assembled repeatably instead of custom-designed one at a time.
  • Designed and integrated an AI-generated visual pipeline in place of traditional photography, to hold consistent visual quality nationwide with no photoshoot lead time per city.
900+PAGES LIVE VIA THE TEMPLATE SYSTEM
TOP 10GOOGLE RANKING WON FOR ACKO DRIVE
TEMPLATIZATION — HOW THE SYSTEM SCALES

One set of components, assembled per city

Rather than design each city's page individually, I broke the page into reusable modules — video hero, reviews, offers, gallery, CTA — that could be reassembled with local content and AI-generated visuals dropped in, without a designer touching each one by hand. That system is what took Acko Drive's organic pages into Google's top-10 rankings and grew organic traffic — and with it, bookings.

08 — Reflect

What I'd take
into the next one

Starting with a fake-door test instead of a finished product changed how I approached every decision after it — I designed the first version to be replaced, not protected. That's a big part of why there were 16 versions of the journey before the one that scaled: none of them needed to be the final answer, only the best answer available at the time.

The hardest problem here was never visual — it was designing certainty for the user when the product itself couldn't offer price certainty. Scaling from one city to a 900+ page nationwide system also changed how I think about "finished": the templatized component system and the AI-assisted visual pipeline mattered as much to the outcome as the original flow decisions, because they're what let one designer keep pace with a product growing faster than its team.
